abstracts.abstract: This study proposes a paradigmatic shift in understanding organizational knowledge dynamics by introducing the Dynamic Knowledge Ecosystem Theory (DKET). Traditional knowledge management frameworks have predominantly treated knowledge as a static, transferable resource, overlooking its emergent and self-organizing properties within complex organizational contexts. Drawing upon complexity theory and distributed cognition, this research conceptualizes knowledge not merely as an asset to be managed but as a living ecosystem characterized by adaptive agents, knowledge niches, and evolutionary learning cycles. Through rigorous conceptual analysis and synthesis of multi-level organizational phenomena, the study identifies three core mechanisms—knowledge symbiosis, adaptive resonance, and emergent integration—that fundamentally govern knowledge creation and evolution in contemporary organizations. The findings reveal that successful knowledge management requires abandoning reductionist transfer models in favor of ecosystem-oriented approaches that cultivate knowledge biodiversity and systemic intelligence. This theoretical contribution redefines the ontological and epistemological foundations of knowledge management strategy, offering scholars and practitioners a novel framework for understanding how intellectual capital generates value through emergent rather than linear processes. The proposed DKET opens unprecedented avenues for investigating knowledge systems as adaptive complexes, fundamentally transforming how organizations conceptualize and implement knowledge management initiatives.

While knowledge sharing has been extensively studied in organizational contexts, existing theoretical models inadequately address the mechanisms underlying knowledge sharing behaviors in digital collaboration platforms. This research extends the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) by integrating constructs from Social Capital Theory and Technology Affordance Framework to develop a comprehensive model of knowledge sharing in technology-mediated environments. Data were collected from 487 knowledge workers across 23 organizations utilizing enterprise collaboration tools, and structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed relationships. The extended model demonstrates substantially improved explanatory power (ΔR² = 0.23) compared to the traditional TPB, with perceived affordance accessibility and relational capital emerging as significant moderators of the intention-behavior gap in digital knowledge exchange. Analysis reveals that technological features that enhance visibility and traceability of contributions significantly strengthen the relationship between attitude and sharing intention. The findings contribute to knowledge management theory by explicating how technological design choices interact with individual motivations and social structures to facilitate or inhibit organizational knowledge flows. This enhanced theoretical framework provides practitioners with evidence-based guidance for optimizing knowledge sharing systems and cultivating cultures that actively promote intellectual capital development through strategic platform design.

This paper presents KnowledgeForge, a groundbreaking knowledge management architecture that fundamentally reimagines organizational knowledge repositories through decentralized ledger technology and artificial intelligence. Conventional knowledge management systems operate on centralized storage paradigms that inherently limit knowledge discovery, create single points of failure, and struggle with knowledge provenance verification. KnowledgeForge introduces a blockchain-based knowledge graph infrastructure where knowledge artifacts are represented as immutable, interconnected nodes within a tamper-proof intellectual capital ledger. The system incorporates semantic reasoning capabilities powered by large language models, enabling natural language queries across distributed knowledge repositories without compromising data sovereignty. A prototype implementation was deployed in a multinational consulting firm comprising 3,200 professionals across 18 countries, serving as a living laboratory for validating the architecture's scalability and effectiveness. Over a six-month evaluation period, the system achieved 94% accuracy in automated knowledge classification, reduced knowledge retrieval time by 67%, and enabled unprecedented traceability of knowledge lineage and attribution. The decentralized design eliminates traditional bottlenecks while ensuring that knowledge contributions remain permanently credited to their creators. This paradigmatic approach to knowledge representation and discovery establishes a new architectural standard for enterprise knowledge systems that prioritizes transparency, resilience, and emergent intelligence over static information storage.

Effective knowledge transfer across organizational boundaries remains a persistent challenge in geographically distributed enterprises, where temporal, cultural, and linguistic barriers frequently impede the flow of intellectual capital. This paper introduces ContextBridge, an enhanced knowledge transfer platform that significantly improves upon existing solutions through context-aware recommendation algorithms and multimodal knowledge encoding. Unlike prior systems that treat knowledge transfer as simple information transmission, ContextBridge recognizes that effective knowledge transfer requires deep contextual adaptation to recipient characteristics, task requirements, and situational constraints. The system employs transformer-based neural networks to analyze recipient learning patterns, cognitive styles, and current project contexts, dynamically generating personalized knowledge packages that optimize comprehension and application. Development involved iterative design science methodology across three organizational case studies, incorporating feedback from 156 knowledge recipients and 43 knowledge providers. Empirical evaluation demonstrated substantial improvements over baseline systems, with knowledge transfer effectiveness increasing by 41% (measured through post-transfer task performance), recipient engagement rising by 58%, and knowledge application accuracy improving by 35%. The multimodal encoding approach, which integrates textual explanations, visual demonstrations, and interactive simulations, proved particularly effective for tacit knowledge transfer. This enhanced platform provides organizations with a powerful tool for accelerating intellectual capital circulation across distributed teams while preserving contextual richness that conventional systems typically lose in transmission.
